title_original: Hank Willis Thomas’s Sleight of Hand
excerpt_original: The artist makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.

blocks.text: Hank Willis Thomas has the rare ability to turn the everyday into a spark, all informed by a mashup of ad-man and bro aesthetics that flips through magazines, dabbles in sports, and repurposes the trappings of nationhood and masculinity. In a seemingly effortless way, he makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.

His skill excites us with the idea that art can communicate to the rest of the world an inner reality negotiated through medium, history, and word play. Sometimes those elements feel meme-like, harvesting popular discourse in a way that frames it for more rarefied spaces like the art museum — his playfulness with All Li v es Matter is a prime example. Other times he’s tapping historical veins for conceptual moments he can elevate or criticize with a little tweak, like the I Am a Man series (2012) that riffs on the Civil Rights protest sign.
